clue.text: Maiden to draw upon?

parts.note: M is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for a maiden over
to draw upon a resource is to use it

explanation.surface: Asks which young woman an artist might take inspiration from.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: a Muse is one of the nine goddess-maidens of Greek myth that poets draw upon for inspiration.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek mythology the Muses were female deities who supplied artists and poets with inspiration.

clue.text: Bloke pressing current party over policy

indicators.note: in a down clue a thing pressing on others lies on top, so it comes first

parts.note: a bloke is a man
I is the physics symbol for electric current
a fest is a festive gathering
O is the cricket abbreviation for over

explanation.surface: A man is pushing the current party line over its policy.
explanation.definitionFit: A manifesto is a published statement of a party's policies and aims.

clue.text: Mean group will engulf large island

indicators.note: to engulf something is to swallow it whole, so it goes inside

parts.note: a squad is a small group
standard abbreviation for large
standard abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A gang is about to overrun a big island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean' is not stingy or average here but shabby and wretched.
explanation.definitionFit: Mean can describe poor, shabby surroundings, and squalid means dirty and wretched in that way.

clue.text: Award for one in respectable address — like a judge?

indicators.note: one thing given for another is swapped in to take its place

parts.note: the Order of the British Empire, a British honour
the Roman numeral for one, the letter swapped out
the polite way to address a man

explanation.surface: Wonders whether a judge might be honoured with a formal title.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the idiom 'sober as a judge'; the question mark marks the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying 'as sober as a judge' makes judges the proverbial model of being clear-headed and serious.

clue.text: Patience is reassessing editorials once the day's passed

indicators.note: reassessing means sorting through again, so the letters are reordered
once the day has gone by it is no longer there, so its letter drops out

parts.note: letters to rearrange
standard abbreviation for day, removed

explanation.surface: Reviewing the leading articles at the end of the day takes patience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Patience' looks like the virtue, but it is the British name for the one-player card game.
explanation.definitionFit: Patience is the British name for card games played alone, which Americans call solitaire.

clue.text: Busy sort and right fool handled pot

parts.note: proverbially busy as a bee
standard abbreviation for right
a mug is a gullible person

explanation.surface: A busy worker and a right idiot dealt with some marijuana.
explanation.walkthrough: 'handled' reads as a verb ending the wordplay, but it describes the pot: a vessel with a handle.
explanation.definitionFit: A beer mug is a drinking vessel with a handle, so a pot with a handle.

clue.text: Honest foundation stripped of leader

indicators.note: losing its leader means the word sheds its opening letter

parts.note: the ground or groundwork is the foundation

explanation.surface: An honest base has had its boss removed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Honest' is an older sense: to be round with someone is to be plain-spoken and candid.
explanation.definitionFit: Round can mean candid and outspoken, as in 'a round rebuke', which is close to honest.

clue.text: Head for top of St Paul's, say

definitions.meaning: first meaning: informal word for the skull or head
second meaning: the great rounded roof of the London cathedral, given as an example

explanation.surface: Directions to make for the highest point of the London cathedral.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head for' reads as 'go towards', but 'Head' is a definition on its own and 'for' merely links it.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang uses the word for a person's head, and Wren's St Paul's Cathedral is famous for its rounded roof of that kind.

clue.text: Is taste in fruit to vanish?

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

parts.note: a date is the fruit of a palm
taken as written
a sip is a small taste of a drink

explanation.surface: A question whether flavour in fruit is meant to fade.
explanation.definitionFit: To dissipate is to disperse or disappear gradually, so to vanish.

clue.text: Ordinary nun made to be different

indicators.note: being made different means changed, so the letters take a new order

parts.note: letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An unremarkable nun is forced to change her ways.
explanation.definitionFit: Mundane means dull and everyday, lacking interest, which is what ordinary means.

clue.text: Fare is new in Europe since I worried about university

parts.note: the French word for new, Europe hinting at a foreign language

indicators.note: about means around, so the rearranged letters go round the next item
something worried is fretted and pulled about, so these letters are disturbed into a new order

parts.note: letters to rearrange
standard abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A traveller frets about a university place since the move to the continent.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters of 'since I' wrap round U after their first letter; 'new in Europe' asks for the French rather than the English word.
explanation.definitionFit: Nouvelle cuisine is a style of cooking with light dishes, so it is a kind of fare, meaning food served.

clue.text: Satisfy French and prepare fish, for example

parts.note: to fill an order or need is to satisfy it
the French word for and

explanation.surface: A cookery instruction: satisfy the diner and get the fish ready.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for example' marks fish as just one thing that can be prepared this way; meat is boned too.
explanation.definitionFit: To fillet is to cut the bones out of fish or meat, a step in preparing it for cooking.

clue.text: Song's flaky with fake adult line

parts.note: flaky is slang for eccentric or crazy
to rig is to fix or falsify a result
A is the film-certificate abbreviation for adult
standard abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A critic dismisses a song as flaky and full of phoney grown-up lines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' just strings the pieces together in order.
explanation.definitionFit: A madrigal is a part-song for several unaccompanied voices, popular in the Renaissance.

clue.text: Knocking out contents of sedan during rip-off

indicators.note: something happening during another event sits within it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a sting is a swindle or confidence trick

indicators.note: the contents of a word are what lies inside it, so its outer letters are dropped

parts.note: the inner letters of the word

explanation.surface: Someone is knocked out in a car while being robbed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocking out' suggests a fight, but here it means putting someone to sleep with a drug.
explanation.definitionFit: Sedating someone with a drug renders them unconscious, which is one sense of knocking them out.

clue.text: It's up in unfavourable market

indicators.note: in a down clue up means reading from the bottom, so the word runs backwards
one thing in another sits inside it

parts.note: adverse means unfavourable or harmful
the word read upwards

explanation.surface: Prices are rising in a poor market.
explanation.walkthrough: 'market' looks like a noun, but it is the verb: to market goods is to promote them.
explanation.definitionFit: To market a product is to promote and publicise it, which is what advertising does.

clue.text: Roofer's rebuke and what starts it

parts.note: to slate is to criticise harshly
'it' stands for the rebuke just named, and what starts that word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A roofer is told off, and the clue asks what began it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' points back to 'rebuke', whose first letter is wanted, not to the word 'it' itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A slater is a tradesman who lays slates on roofs, so a roofer.

clue.text: Firm is straight with popular bloke

parts.note: STR is a recognised abbreviation for straight
in fashion, so popular
a gent is a gentleman, a man

explanation.surface: A company is honest and has a well-liked man in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like a business, but it is the adjective meaning strict.
explanation.definitionFit: Stringent rules are strict and rigorous, so firm in the sense of unyielding.

clue.text: On edge over northern church's home

indicators.note: in a down clue a thing over another sits above it, so it comes first

parts.note: re means on or concerning
the side of something is its edge
standard abbreviation for northern
the Church of England

explanation.surface: A nervous person worries about the vicarage of a northern church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On edge' reads as nervous, but the two words are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A residence is the place where someone lives, a home.

clue.text: Canon's man avoiding tactical ruse

indicators.note: the tactic steers clear of the named word, so those letters are left out

parts.note: a manoeuvre is a clever tactical move
taken as written, the letters removed

explanation.surface: A clergyman dodging some tactical trick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Canon' looks like a churchman, but it is the body of an author's works.
explanation.definitionFit: A canon is the complete body of an artist's works, which is also what the borrowed French word for a life's work means.

clue.text: Sensing fluttering flags

indicators.note: fluttering things flap about, so the letters are tossed into a new order

parts.note: letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone senses flags waving in the wind.
explanation.definitionFit: Ensigns are flags, especially those flown by ships to show nationality.

clue.text: Hellish watchdog backing unmistakable second-class record

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the string is read from its end

parts.note: something sure is certain, beyond mistake
B grade is second class
standard abbreviation for record

explanation.surface: A guard dog supporting a clearly mediocre record.
explanation.definitionFit: Cerberus is the three-headed dog of Greek myth that guards the gates of Hades, the underworld.

clue.text: Had copyright worked up

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for copyright, as in the © symbol
heated means angry or agitated

explanation.surface: Someone owned a copyright and got angry about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Had' looks like the past of 'have', but it is the slang sense of being conned.
explanation.definitionFit: To be had is informal for being tricked or swindled, so had means cheated.

clue.text: Source of dismay in repeat struggles?

definitions.text: Source of dismay in repeat struggles?

indicators.note: something that struggles writhes about, so these letters are twisted into a new order
the source of a word is where it begins, its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter
letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Asks what causes dismay in endless repeated struggles.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: bureaucracy is what dismays people battling the same forms again and again.
explanation.definitionFit: Red tape is excessive bureaucratic procedure, notorious for frustrating people who have to deal with it.

clue.text: Sure strange term for access code?

indicators.note: strange means odd or out of the ordinary, so these letters come out in an unusual order

parts.note: letters to rearrange
a term is a name for something

explanation.surface: Someone finds an unusual word to use for a password.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is loose: the login name is only half of the code that grants access.
explanation.definitionFit: A username is the identifier typed in to log on to a computer system, part of the credentials for access.

clue.text: Confused in the main?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: bewildered, not knowing what to do
second meaning: on the ocean, the main being a poetic word for the sea

explanation.walkthrough: 'in the main' usually means mostly; the question mark flags the old sense of main as the open sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on the ocean is literal, and the idiom extends it to being lost and bewildered.

clue.text: What Homer sometimes did is agreed

definitions.meaning: first meaning: from Horace's saying that even good Homer nods, i.e. slips up or dozes
second meaning: showed assent with a dip of the head

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'even Homer nods' says the greatest writers sometimes lapse; the past tense suits 'did'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dipping the head is a gesture of assent, and in the proverb the poet dozing off stands for a lapse in attention.

clue.text: How is Prohibitionist contrary to expectations?

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read cryptically: someone banning drink opposes grain spirit and beer
second meaning: going against one's natural inclination or the norm

explanation.walkthrough: Grain here is the cereal that whisky and beer are made from, so a teetotal campaigner is literally opposed to it.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom comes from cutting wood across its fibres, and means acting against what is natural or expected.

clue.text: Dogs possibly seen in Paisley

indicators.note: something seen in a word is visible inside it, sitting among its letters

parts.note: the inner run of letters of the Scottish town's name

explanation.surface: Dogs might be spotted in the Scottish town of Paisley.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Dogs is a district of East London; 'possibly' flags it as one example of such a place.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Dogs in London is one named island, so 'Dogs' stands for an example of the word.

clue.text: Check motor, close to clapped-out

parts.note: an Audi is a make of car

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is used

parts.note: the final letter

explanation.surface: A mechanic is asked to check a car that is nearly worn out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clapped-out' is British slang for worn out, typically of an old car.
explanation.definitionFit: An audit is an official inspection of accounts, a formal check.

clue.text: Perhaps fair time in charge

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

parts.note: a charge or payment
standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Perhaps the moment has come for a fair-minded person to be put in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fair' reads as an adjective, but it is a noun: a fair is one kind of outdoor festivity.
explanation.definitionFit: A fete is an outdoor fundraising event with stalls and games, much like a fair.
